title: Dialects 方言
intro: Textbooks teach 標準語, and then you meet someone from Osaka and catch about half of it. Almost none of that gap is new vocabulary — it is the same grammar wearing different endings: だ becomes や, ない becomes へん, いい becomes ええ. Learn the swaps and Kansai stops being a foreign language. After that come the words that have no standard equivalent, and a tour of the rest of the country so you can place a voice on a map.

stages.name: Kansai: the system
stages.note: The mechanical swaps. Do this as soon as you can hold a plain-form conversation — most of it is relabelling grammar you already have.

stages.name: Kansai: the feel
stages.note: Vocabulary, sentence endings, pitch and register. Where it stops being a code and starts being a voice.

stages.name: The rest of Japan
stages.note: Recognition, not production. The goal is to hear a form and know roughly where the speaker is from.

modules.title: The Kansai swaps 関西の文法
modules.blurb: Fifteen substitutions that convert most of what you know into Kansai-ben. Drill them until the conversion is automatic.
modules.note: Kansai-ben is not broken Japanese or slang. It is a full system with its own copula, negatives and sound changes, and in Osaka it is what educated adults speak to each other all day.

items.note: One syllable carries most of the dialect. だから→やから, だけど→やけど, だろう→やろ, なんだ→なんや.
せや is the Osaka default; そや and ほや also occur. ほな (= それじゃあ) uses the same ほ: ほな、また明日.
Kansai has no everyday polite copula of its own — です does the job. どす (Kyoto) and だす (old Osaka) are period-drama costume; using them is like saying 'prithee'.
Only the dictionary form changes. The past is still よかった, and the negative is ようない (よくない is heard too). ええ天気やな.
〜てる is neutral. 〜とる is rougher and more male in Osaka — 何しとん？ can land as a challenge where 何してん？ does not.
Past 〜てもた: 忘れてもた. Tokyo's 〜ちゃった is understood perfectly well in Kansai but sounds imported. Separately, note that standalone ちゃう in Kansai is 違う — a different word that only looks related.
行かなあかん. There is no everyday polite version — for 〜なければなりません even lifelong Osakans switch to 標準語.
触ったらあかんで. あかん covers everything だめ covers.
行かんでもええ. The plain Kansai negative stem is 〜ん: 知らん, わからん, 行かん.
やろ？ fishes for agreement, やろな muses. It is plain speech — not a stand-in for でしょう with someone senior.
どないする？, どないしたん？, どないやねん. どう is still said; どない is the marked local one.
Kansai keeps the old ウ音便 — adverbial 〜く becomes 〜う and fuses. 早く→はよう→はよ, よく→よう. はよ行こ.
The same change before なる: 安くなる→やすうなる. Strongest in older speakers; younger Osakans often just say 高くなる.
う-verbs take ウ音便 in the past and the て-form: 言うた (ゆうた), 買うてくる, 思うてた. The change learners never notice they are missing.

For 一段 verbs and する the Kansai imperative is the ます-stem, usually softened with や: はよしいや, ちょっと見いや. 五段 verbs keep the standard imperative — 行け, 飲め — and take や on the stem instead: 行きや. Downward only, parent to child or friend to friend.

modules.title: Negatives in へん 否定
modules.blurb: Kansai has two negatives where Tokyo has one: the everyday 〜へん and the shorter 〜ん. This is the module that unlocks listening.
modules.note: 〜へん is the conversational default and 〜ん is shorter and blunter, but both are ordinary speech — neither is rude. The irregular verbs (する, 来る, できる) are where the city you learned in shows. The last two rows are the odd ones out: the negative request and the copula negative are built on 〜ん and ちゃう, not on 〜へん.

items.note: For 五段 verbs 〜へん sits on the same stem as 〜ない. Osaka also says 行けへん for this — it looks like the potential and is not.
わからん and 知らん are the everyday forms; the へん versions come out a little softer.
一段 verbs drop る and add へん: 寝へん, 起きへん.
After an い vowel へん often becomes ひん and the stem stretches: 見いひん, 起きひん, できひん. This is a tendency, not a rule — 見えへん is just as current in Osaka — and Kyoto uses ひん more widely than Osaka does.
せえへん is Osaka, しいひん Kyoto, せん the wider western form. All three are current.
こーへん is Osaka, きーひん Kyoto, けーへん Kobe. This one word tells a local exactly where you learned your Japanese.
ある has no 〜ん negative of its own — plain ない does that job. あらへん and あれへん are the same emphatic word, where ない is flat.
The stem shifts to でけ〜, not でき〜 — though younger speakers do say できひん.
〜とらん is the negative of 〜とる: rougher in Osaka, but the normal form further west.
Both are built on 〜ん, not on へん, and both are warm rather than sharp: 言わんといてや. If anything 〜んとって is the more coaxing of the two, not the blunter.
Kansai adds かった to the whole negative instead of inflecting ない.
Neither of these is a へん form: そうちゃう uses ちゃう (= 違う) and そうやない is や + ない. Both are current, and ちゃう also stands alone as a flat 'no, wrong'.

modules.title: The sound of Kansai 音とアクセント
modules.blurb: The vocabulary is the easy half. Pitch, vowel length and rhythm are what actually mark a speaker — and what makes a bad screen Kansai sound fake.

items.note: Tokyo drops the pitch on 雨 and leaves 飴 rising. Kansai reverses the pair — there it is 飴 that falls. Kansai is not 'accentless'; it is a different accent system, and a more conservative one than Tokyo's.

A large class of two-mora words that are low-then-high in Tokyo start high in Kansai: 犬, 山, 花, 川. This is what a local registers first, long before your vocabulary. Do not extend it to 猫 — 猫 already starts high in Tokyo.
One-mora nouns get stretched: 木ぃ, 目ぇ, 手ぇ, 血ぃ. 気ぃつけて, 手ぇ貸して. A short clipped き sounds like a newsreader.
Tokyo devoices the high vowels — s'ki des'. Kansai voices them: su-ki-de-su, with the す audible at the end. Nothing else changes how local you sound for so little effort.
Long vowels are held their full length and doubled consonants are really doubled — ええ is two beats, めっちゃ has a real stop in the middle. Clip them and the word stops sounding Kansai.
Kansai moves through a wider pitch range and the sentence rises and falls more. Flat delivery is what gives away an actor doing Kansai — not the words.

items.ja: ちゃうちゃうちゃうんちゃう？
items.r: ちゃうちゃうちゃうんちゃう？
items.en: That's not a Chow Chow, is it?
items.note: The famous Kansai tongue-twister: ちゃうちゃう (Chow Chow) + ちゃう (isn't) + んちゃう？ (…is it?). Four ちゃう doing three different jobs, separated only by pitch and timing. If you can hear this one, your ear has arrived.

modules.title: Sentence endings 文末
modules.blurb: ねん, やん, で, な, わ. The endings carry the attitude, and they are the fastest way to sound either native or like a tourist doing an impression.
modules.note: These are plain speech. Every one of them is out of place with a customer, a client or anyone much senior — in those situations Kansai speakers use 標準語 keigo like everyone else.

items.note: ねん is 〜んだ/〜のだ — it explains rather than just states. The most Kansai-marking ending there is, and the one learners overuse first.
The question form of ねん is bare 〜ん？ with a rise. 何してん？ = 何してるの？
やん = じゃない(か) and clips onto plain forms: ええやん, 行くやん. やんか pushes back: 言うたやんか, 'I did tell you.'
で is Kansai's よ — informing, not swaggering. Unlike Tokyo's ぜ it is used by women and older speakers just as much.
な does the work of ね throughout: ええ天気やな, 疲れたな.
Kansai わ is flat and gender-neutral, and men use it constantly. It is not the rising, feminine わ of Tokyo speech.
やんな asks for confirmation; やろ？ assumes it.
〜か on the volitional is a soft invitation: ぼちぼち行こか.
〜て is 〜って — reporting or insisting. 言うてるやん, 'I keep telling you.'
〜えな and 〜や turn a request into a wheedle: 教えてえな, 見してや. Friends only; it sounds childish upwards.

items.en: What the hell are you doing?
items.note: The loud comic register of 漫才 and arguments. From a learner it reads as an impression rather than speech.
がな is heavy old-Osaka — mostly older men and comedians now. Understand it; you do not need it.

modules.title: Kansai vocabulary 語彙
modules.blurb: The words with no clean standard equivalent, plus the false friends that will genuinely mislead you. Learn these and you understand most of what you hear.

items.note: ほんま is 本当, ほんまに is 本当に. If you take one word from this track, take this one — it is everywhere.

items.en: Damn, I'm going to be late.
items.note: あかん does the work of だめ: no good, don't, must not. 〜たらあかん (must not), 〜なあかん (have to). Far more common in Kansai than だめ.

items.ja: めっちゃおいしいやん。
items.r: めっちゃおいしいやん。
items.note: Kansai slang that has gone nationwide in casual speech, and nowadays in casual writing too — but still not in formal writing and not to anyone senior.
The 漫才 retort to something absurd, usually with a light slap on the arm. Playful between friends; chilly if you aim it at someone you barely know.

items.ja: ちゃうちゃう、そうやなくて。
items.r: ちゃうちゃう、そうやなくて。
items.en: No no, that's not what I mean.
items.note: ちゃう = 違う. On the end of a sentence it becomes 〜じゃない？: 明日ちゃう？ 'It's tomorrow, isn't it?'
Drained in body or mind — heavier than 疲れた, and also used of a task: しんどい仕事, a slog. Understood nationwide now.
= 仕方ない. The everyday Kansai shrug, said far more often than しょうがない is in Tokyo.

items.en: No problem, don't worry about it.
items.note: = 構わない. The standard thing to say when someone apologises to you.
Genuine, but increasingly the mark of shopkeepers, older speakers and Kyoto. Young Osakans say ありがとう or サンキュー. Safe to understand; slightly costume-y to use.
The textbook 'Osaka greeting' — a merchant-era cliché from comedy and tourist posters that essentially no one says. The scripted reply is ぼちぼちでんな. Know them, don't use them.
Unlike もうかりまっか, ぼちぼち is alive and everywhere: so-so, little by little, or 'about time we moved'.
= いくら. Blunt and friendly — fine in a market or with friends, out of place in a department store. Also ordinary in Tohoku and Hokkaido, so it is not a Kansai giveaway on its own.
おもろい = おもしろい. In Kansai calling someone おもろい is real praise; おもんない is close to an insult.

items.ja: あの店、美味しいで。知らんけど。
items.r: あのみせ、おいしいで。しらんけど。
items.en: That place is good. Not that I'd know.
items.note: 知らんけど is tacked onto a confident statement to disclaim all responsibility for it. A genuine Osaka verbal tic that became a national meme.
ええで grants permission. Careful with ええわ — depending on tone it means 'that's fine' or 'no thanks', and learners pick the wrong one.

items.en: Are you out of your mind?
items.note: In Kansai あほ is often affectionate and ばか is the harsh one — the reverse of Tokyo, where ばか is light and あほ stings. Still an insult: recognise it, don't try it.
The worst false friend in the dialect: in Kansai なおす means put away, not repair. Say it in Tokyo and your colleague takes the thing off to be fixed.
ほかす = 捨てる. 〜といて is 〜ておいて.
えらい in Kansai means 'awfully' or 'gruelling', not 'admirable': えらい人多いな, 'wow, it's packed'. こっちゃ = ことだ.
Osaka attaches ちゃん and さん to everyday things — 飴ちゃん, お豆さん, お粥さん. The 飴ちゃん produced from an older woman's handbag is a genuine institution.

modules.title: Politeness in Kansai 敬語とはる
modules.blurb: Kansai has its own light respectful form, 〜はる — and its own rules about when to drop the dialect entirely.

items.ja: 先生、もう帰らはったで。
items.r: せんせい、もうかえらはったで。
items.note: 〜はる is Kansai's own respectful ending, much lighter than 尊敬語 — closer in weight to です・ます. In Kyoto it gets used about neighbours, customers, even the cat.

items.ja: 田中さん、何してはるん？
items.r: たなかさん、なにしてはるん？
items.note: The stem differs by city. For 五段 verbs Osaka attaches はる to the ない-stem — 行かはる, 帰らはる, 読まはる — while Kyoto uses the ます-stem: 行きはる, 帰りはる. 一段 verbs and する take the ます-stem either way: 食べはる, 見はる, しはる. Kyoto attaches it to almost anything; Osaka uses it more sparingly.

items.ja: お客さん、何にしはりますか。
items.r: おきゃくさん、なににしはりますか。
items.note: はります is the polite form. Kyoto shop staff use it all day for a job that would need なさいますか in Tokyo.
The Kyoto shop-front greeting; おこしやす is the warmer one, for a guest who was expected. Lovely to hear, costume-y from a visitor.
かんにん is Kansai's ごめん. Softer and more familiar than すみません, and used inside families and between friends — never to a client or anyone senior.
でっか, まっせ and まんねん are merchant Osaka — instantly recognisable and now almost purely a comedian's costume. Understand them; don't wear them.

items.ja: いつもお世話になっております。
items.r: いつもおせわになっております。
items.note: Business Japanese in Osaka is 標準語 keigo, identical to Tokyo's. Kansai-ben belongs in the corridor, not in front of the client — locals switch too.
Warm and everyday between colleagues and friends. Note the stretched 気ぃ — 手ぇ, 目ぇ and 血ぃ do the same.

items.r: かんさいべん、じょうずやね。
items.note: What you will be told, kindly, the first time you try. Kansai people enjoy a foreigner speaking their dialect — but keep 標準語 for anyone senior, because polite Kansai is the hard part.

modules.title: A tour of the dialects 全国編
modules.blurb: Two or three signature markers from each of the big dialect regions — enough to recognise them on television and to know when a word means something else entirely.
modules.note: Some of these are alive and ordinary; some are what television thinks a region sounds like. The notes say which.

items.note: んだんだ as agreement. The most recognisable Tohoku word there is.
〜べ marks intention or a guess; the copula version is 〜だべ. The く→ぐ voicing between vowels is Tohoku specifically — North Kanto says 行くべ.
さ replaces へ and に. Tohoku speech is sometimes subtitled on national television, which locals find as patronising as it sounds.
Not 'scary'. A real false friend that causes real confusion.
なまら is the Hokkaido intensifier. 〜っしょ (from でしょ) is the other giveaway.
ゴミ投げといて means bin it, not hurl it.
〜たい states the speaker's own view; 〜ばい presents it to the listener as news. Both are everyday Hakata.

items.en: I like it / I like you
items.note: 好いとう (好いとぉ) is the statement. Add と for the question: 好いとーと？ — 〜と？ is the general Kyushu question ending, as in 行くと？
The widest western marker of all — Fukuoka to Matsuyama to Hiroshima.
ばり is Hakata's intensifier, and 〜か is the local adjective ending (速か, よか). Osaka would say めっちゃ, Hiroshima ぶち.
じゃけえ ('because') is the signature. Gangster films made 広島弁 the voice of screen yakuza; it is an ordinary regional dialect with an unfair reputation.
ぶち is the local とても: ぶちうまい, ぶち寒い.
だがや and みゃー are the television version. Actual Nagoya speech today is close to 標準語, with 〜だがね and 〜がや surviving in casual talk.
Where Osaka says あかん.
Three regions, three meanings: Nagoya えらい = tired, Kansai えらい = awfully (えらい人多いな), standard えらい = admirable. Context decides which one you are hearing.
Okinawan is not a dialect the way Kansai is — it separated early enough that the two are not mutually intelligible. It gets a module of its own in this stage.

modules.title: Placing what you hear 出身当て
modules.blurb: Hear an ending, place the speaker. This is the practical skill — you will never say most of these, and you do not need to.
modules.note: Boundaries are soft and people move, so treat these as a first guess rather than a verdict. One ending plus one vocabulary item is usually enough to get the region right.

items.note: The eastern twin of やん, from the Tokai coast and Yokohama before Tokyo took it up.
でしょ worn flat. It has leaked into general casual speech, so wait for なまら before you call Hokkaido on it.

items.where: 北海道・東北・北関東

items.note: A real Sendai-area ending (also Sado), but most people meet the stylised version Lum speaks in Urusei Yatsura first — which is why anime fans place it anywhere but Sendai.
A genuine older-male ね in western Japan. It is also the all-purpose 'old man' ending of period drama and manga, which is why it sounds archaic even when it is real speech.
ずら sounds archaic even locally now; だら is still in daily use.

modules.title: Okinawan うちなーぐち 沖縄
modules.blurb: Not a dialect but a related language, plus the Okinawan-flavoured Japanese that everyone actually speaks. One item here will save you genuine embarrassment.

items.note: On every shop door and at the airport. Okinawan and Japanese split far enough back that a Tokyo speaker understands almost none of the real language.
Said by men; women say はいたい. Friendly and a little performed these days — roughly 'howdy'.
Formal Okinawan. In daily life people say ありがとう; this turns up in speeches, songs and to visitors.
The full saying is まくとぅそーけー なんくるないさ — 'do the right thing and it will work out'. It means keep going, not don't bother; the souvenir-T-shirt reading irritates people.
ちゅら = 清ら, beautiful. The aquarium writes it 美ら海 with 美.
The all-purpose agreement of Okinawan Japanese — and often the whole turn, with nothing following. Mainlanders keep waiting for the rest of the sentence.

items.r: もうかえりましょうね。
items.note: The trap. In Okinawa 〜ましょうね announces what the speaker is about to do alone. Mainlanders hear an invitation and follow them out of the door.
= 頑張れ. Shouted at 甲子園 and at anyone facing a hard day.

items.ja: うちなーんちゅ・やまとんちゅ
items.r: うちなーんちゅ、やまとんちゅ
items.note: 〜んちゅ is 〜の人. Worth knowing which one you are in the conversation you are listening to.
